# ASC 852-10 — reorganizations; fresh-start reporting

*Citation:* FASB ASC 852-10-45-19 through 45-29; 852-10-45-9  
*Status in this library:* in force

Fresh-start reporting is applied upon emergence **only if both** conditions are met: (a) the reorganization value of the assets of the emerging entity immediately before the date of confirmation is **less than** the total of all post-petition liabilities and allowed claims; **and** (b) holders of existing voting shares immediately before confirmation receive **less than 50 percent** of the voting shares of the emerging entity. If either condition fails, the entity does not adopt fresh-start reporting; liabilities compromised by the plan are stated at present value of amounts to be paid and the **gain on discharge is reported as a reorganization item** in the income statement. During the case, liabilities subject to compromise are reported separately from post-petition liabilities (852-10-45-4 to 45-6); pre-petition liabilities are not netted against post-petition assets.

# Bankruptcy Code — automatic stay, use of property, administrative expenses, post-petition transfers

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §§362(a), 363(b)-(c), 503(b), 549(a)  
*Status in this library:* in force

§549(a): the trustee (debtor in possession) may avoid a transfer of property of the estate that occurs after the commencement of the case and is not authorized by the Code or by the court. **Payment of a pre-petition unsecured claim outside the ordinary course and without a court order is an unauthorized post-petition transfer** (and may be recovered from the recipient). §503(b)(1): actual, necessary costs of preserving the estate after the petition (post-petition goods and services) are administrative expenses payable in the ordinary course. §363(c)(1): ordinary-course transactions need no court approval; §363(b): non-ordinary-course use requires notice and hearing.

# Bankruptcy Code §507(a)(4) — wage priority

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §507(a)(4)

Allowed unsecured claims for wages, salaries or commissions earned within 180 days before the petition, up to $17,150 per individual (as adjusted), have fourth priority. Payment of pre-petition wages during the case requires a court order (first-day wage motion).

# IRC §108 — income from discharge of indebtedness; reduction of tax attributes

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §108(a)(1)(A), (b)(1)-(5)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a)(1)(A) Gross income does not include any amount which would be includible by reason of the discharge of indebtedness of the taxpayer if the discharge occurs in a title 11 case. (b)(1) The amount excluded **shall be applied to reduce the tax attributes** of the taxpayer in this order: (A) net operating losses (the NOL for the year of discharge and carryovers), (B) general business credits, (C) minimum tax credit, (D) capital loss carryovers, (E) basis of property, (F) passive activity loss carryovers, (G) foreign tax credits. Reductions are made after the tax for the year of discharge is determined. (b)(5) The taxpayer may elect to apply any portion of the reduction first to the basis of depreciable property.

# ASC 852-10 — reorganizations; fresh-start reporting

*Citation:* FASB ASC 852-10-45-19 through 45-29; 852-10-45-9  
*Status in this library:* in force

Fresh-start reporting is applied upon emergence **only if both** conditions are met: (a) the reorganization value of the assets of the emerging entity immediately before the date of confirmation is **less than** the total of all post-petition liabilities and allowed claims; **and** (b) holders of existing voting shares immediately before confirmation receive **less than 50 percent** of the voting shares of the emerging entity. If either condition fails, the entity does not adopt fresh-start reporting; liabilities compromised by the plan are stated at present value of amounts to be paid and the **gain on discharge is reported as a reorganization item** in the income statement. During the case, liabilities subject to compromise are reported separately from post-petition liabilities (852-10-45-4 to 45-6); pre-petition liabilities are not netted against post-petition assets.

===== bc_330_331.md =====
# Bankruptcy Code §§330, 331 — compensation of professionals

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §§330(a), 331  
*Status in this library:* in force

Professionals employed under §327 are paid only upon application and court award (§330) or under interim compensation procedures ordered by the court (§331). Payments outside those procedures are subject to disgorgement.

===== bc_362_363_503_549.md =====
# Bankruptcy Code — automatic stay, use of property, administrative expenses, post-petition transfers

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §§362(a), 363(b)-(c), 503(b), 549(a)  
*Status in this library:* in force

§549(a): the trustee (debtor in possession) may avoid a transfer of property of the estate that occurs after the commencement of the case and is not authorized by the Code or by the court. **Payment of a pre-petition unsecured claim outside the ordinary course and without a court order is an unauthorized post-petition transfer** (and may be recovered from the recipient). §503(b)(1): actual, necessary costs of preserving the estate after the petition (post-petition goods and services) are administrative expenses payable in the ordinary course. §363(c)(1): ordinary-course transactions need no court approval; §363(b): non-ordinary-course use requires notice and hearing.

# Bankruptcy Code §507(a)(4) — wage priority

*Citation:* 11 U.S.C. §507(a)(4)  
*Status in this library:* in force

Allowed unsecured claims for wages, salaries or commissions earned within 180 days before the petition, up to $17,150 per individual (as adjusted), have fourth priority. Payment of pre-petition wages during the case requires a court order (first-day wage motion).

# IRC §108 — income from discharge of indebtedness; reduction of tax attributes

*Citation:* 26 U.S.C. §108(a)(1)(A), (b)(1)-(5)  
*Status in this library:* in force

(a)(1)(A) Gross income does not include any amount which would be includible by reason of the discharge of indebtedness of the taxpayer if the discharge occurs in a title 11 case. (b)(1) The amount excluded **shall be applied to reduce the tax attributes** of the taxpayer in this order: (A) net operating losses (the NOL for the year of discharge and carryovers), (B) general business credits, (C) minimum tax credit, (D) capital loss carryovers, (E) basis of property, (F) passive activity loss carryovers, (G) foreign tax credits. Reductions are made after the tax for the year of discharge is determined. (b)(5) The taxpayer may elect to apply any portion of the reduction first to the basis of depreciable property.

# Memo / reply to CFO email of 2026-03-19 ("Mesa Steel — just pay them")

**From:** Controller
**To:** Gil Ferreira, CFO
**Date:** 2026-03-27
**Re:** Mesa February invoice, netting proposal, and Holland & Pierce $140,000 — answers with authority

Gil — short answer: we cannot pay the Mesa February invoice, we cannot net it, and we cannot pay Holland &
Pierce yet. Each is blocked by a Court order that is already entered in our case, not by a general rule. I
set out below why, and the lawful path to the steel, which is faster than it looks.

---

## 1. "Pay the Mesa Feb invoice ($62,400) out of the DIP draw this week" — **No.**

**(a) The Final DIP Order (Dkt. 61) forbids it.** DIP proceeds "shall be used solely for post-petition
operating expenses, administrative expenses allowed by the Court, and the Carve-Out. Nothing herein
authorizes payment of any pre-petition claim except as separately ordered by this Court" (Dkt. 61 ¶2). The
February invoice is a pre-petition claim; no order separately allows it.

**(b) The critical-vendor order (Dkt. 48) does not cover Mesa.** Its Schedule 1 lists **only Apex Coatings,
Inc. ($31,200.00)**, "No other vendor is included. Any motion to add a vendor requires notice and a
hearing." Also note the order's cap is **$35,000 in the aggregate**, and Apex's $31,200 payment (made
3/24) has already consumed all but **$3,800** of it — so even adding Mesa requires an amended order
raising the aggregate cap, not just adding a name.

**(c) The Bankruptcy Code independently blocks it.** The Mesa February claim is a pre-petition general
unsecured claim, subject to the automatic stay, 11 U.S.C. §362(a) (library: `bc_362_363_503_549.md`). A
payment of a pre-petition unsecured claim outside the ordinary course and without a court order is an
**unauthorized post-petition transfer** the estate can avoid under 11 U.S.C. §549(a) — and could be
**recovered back from Mesa**. Paying them would buy leverage we lose twice: the money comes back and
Mesa ends up having to give back the payment. A payment "we'll explain later" is exactly the fact pattern
§549(a) is written for.

**(d) What we *can* do for Mesa this week — and should:**
- Mesa's **post-petition deliveries are administrative expenses** — "actual, necessary costs of preserving
  the estate" under 11 U.S.C. §503(b)(1) — and ordinary-course transactions need no court approval,
  11 U.S.C. §363(c)(1). Their 3/18 delivery invoice of **$18,900 is unpaid and payable now** in the
  ordinary course. Paying it promptly is lawful, immediate, and shows good faith.
- Q2 structural steel Mesa ships **after** the petition will likewise be an administrative expense paid in
  the ordinary course. That is real assurance we can give them today, backed by the Code.
- If Mesa still insists on the February balance, the **lawful route** Dkt. 48 itself contemplates is a
  noticed motion to add Mesa to Schedule 1 and raise the $35,000 aggregate cap, conditioned on Mesa
  agreeing in writing to Customary Trade Terms for the case (Dkt. 48 ¶1). If you want this, I will
  prepare the motion facts today and route them to Corbin/the restructuring team for filing — with
  notice and a hearing, per Dkt. 48. The Denver Water contract is a good argument for "critical"; it
  just has to go through the judge, not around her.
- If Mesa will not ship absent the illegal payment, that is leverage the **plan** provides, not the wire:
  the term sheet gives unsecured creditors 35% cash over 24 months; Mesa's February claim sits in that
  pool and cannot be preferentially paid now.

permitted."** Netting is just payment of the February invoice by arithmetic: we would be disbursing DIP
dollars (a portion of the $62,400 equal to the invoice, reduced by the coil credit) on a pre-petition
claim. It fails ¶2 and ¶3 of Dkt. 61 and has the same §549(a) exposure. What we *can* do: collect the
coil credit from Mesa as a normal post-petition account receivable (it would be reported as a receipt),
while the February invoice stays unpaid and un-paids itself into the claims pool. Please tell me the
coil credit amount so I can record it — it is not in the file (see QUESTIONS.md).

Professionals employed under §327 are paid **only upon application and court award (11 U.S.C. §330(a))
or under interim compensation procedures ordered by the Court (11 U.S.C. §331)**; payments outside
those procedures are **subject to disgorgement** (library: `bc_330_331.md`). Paying first and telling
them after puts the firm's fees at risk of being handed back and puts the transfer itself under §549(a).
There is no "ask forgiveness" version of this for professionals.

## 4. "Can you pay Holland & Pierce their $140k?" — **Not now; soon, through the right channel.**

As of 3/31 no fee application for the $140,000 has been granted, so there is no award and no authority
to pay: §§330(a), 331. The **interim compensation order entered 4/14 (80% paid / 100% holdback regime)**
is the channel — once that procedure is running, H&P gets paid under it, and I will report approved /
paid / held back in the April MOR (Part 5). Corbin Advisors' $45,000 is in the same posture: fee
application required before any payment. As of the March 31 cutoff, Part 5 shows **$0 approved, $0
paid, $0 held back** — nothing had been awarded or paid during March.

---

- Paid in March, all authorized: payroll $412,000 (pre-petition portion within the §507(a)(4) per-employee

  §503(b)(1)/§363(c)(1)); Apex pre-petition $31,200 (Dkt. 48, within its cap); utilities deposit $28,000
  (Dkt. 31).
- **Not** paid, and correctly so: Mesa February $62,400; Front Range pre-petition $7,400; Grainger
  pre-petition $4,310 — these are "liabilities subject to compromise." Holland & Pierce $140,000 and
  Corbin $45,000 — post-petition payables awaiting §§330/331 procedures. Mesa post-petition $18,900 —
  payable now; **recommend we pay it this week.**
- Part 7 of the MOR honestly answers: payments on pre-petition debt — **Yes** (Apex $31,200 per Dkt. 48;
  capped pre-petition wages per Dkt. 9), each with docket reference; payments outside the ordinary course
  without approval — **No.**

If Mesa won't move, call the restructuring team today about the Dkt. 48 amendment. I'll have the vendor
facts and the Denver Water exposure ready to attach.

— Controller

*All statutory citations above are to the reference library indexed at `library/INDEX.md` (only items in that index were relied on). Docket references are to our case file orders in `documents/`.*
